extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/college students learning introductory discrete mathematics (logic and counting)
extracted.subtask_description: Introductory textbook guidance on basic propositional logic (rules of inference, DeMorgan, parsing quantifiers) and elementary counting (lists, multiplication principle, permutations, combinations, Pascal's triangle, binomial theorem) with worked examples and exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modus Ponens (logical inference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose we know that a statement of form P => Q is true. This tells us that whenever P is true, Q will also be true. If in addition we happen to know that P is true then it must be that Q is true. This is called a logical inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represented by stacking P => Q and P above a line with Q below. Use truth tables to verify such inferences. Example/formal pattern: from P^>Q and P infer Q (modus ponens).

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic propositional inference rules (conjunction/disjunction/negation)
rubrics_metrics.description: If P and Q are both true then the statement P ∧ Q will be true. Conversely, P ∧ Q being true forces P (and also Q) to be true. If P is true, then P ∨ Q must be true, no matter what Q is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These inferences follow directly from truth tables and are used frequently in proofs. The text lists these intuitive inference patterns (conjunction introduction/elimination, disjunction introduction, etc.) and encourages familiarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use DeMorgan's laws and logical equivalences
rubrics_metrics.description: Logical rules such as DeMorgan's laws help correctly change certain statements into (potentially more useful) statements with the same meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use equivalences to rewrite statements (e.g., move negation past quantifiers or connectives) to clarify meaning or make statements easier to manipulate in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parse mathematical sentences with precise logical meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The truth tables we studied tell us the exact meanings of words such as 'and,' 'or', 'not' and so on. Whenever we use or read the 'If..., then' construction in a mathematical context, logic tells us exactly what is meant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reading/writing mathematical sentences, mentally translate to logical symbols (∧, ∨, →, ¬, ∀, ∃) to avoid ambiguity; logic is the background language of mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a list (ordered sequence) and equality
rubrics_metrics.description: A list is an ordered sequence of objects denoted (a,b,c,...). Entries have a definite order; rearranging entries produces a different list. Lists may have repeated entries. The number of entries is the length. The empty list () has length zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use parentheses and commas to avoid ambiguity (e.g., (9,10,11) is not the same as 91011). Two lists are equal only if they have the same entries in the same order and same length. Nested lists and lists of sets are allowed; examples illustrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication Principle (product rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose in making a list of length n there are a1 possible choices for the first entry, a2 possible choices for the second, ..., an possible choices for the nth entry. Then the total number of different lists that can be made this way is the product a1·a2·...·an.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a tree-diagram or sequential reasoning to count choices. Examples: lists with choices 3,2,2 give 3·2·2 = 12; license plate example (3 letters then 4 digits) yields 26·26·26·10·10·10·10 = 17,576,000.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting with repetition (n^k for length-k lists)
rubrics_metrics.description: When repetition is allowed and there are n possible symbols for each entry, the number of length-k lists is n^k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in examples like 7^4 when 7 possible letters and repetition allowed. Useful baseline for complementary counting and subtractive methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting without repetition — permutations (n(n-1)...(n-k+1) = n!/(n-k)!)
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of non-repetitive lists of length k whose entries are chosen from a set of n possible entries is n(n-1)(n-2)...(n-k+1), which can be written n!/(n-k)!.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived via the Multiplication Principle by decrementing available choices after each selection. Example: number of non-repetitive length-n lists from n symbols is n!.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorial definition and recurrence (n! and 0! = 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If n is a non-negative integer, n! (n factorial) is the number of non-repetitive lists of length n that can be made from n symbols. Thus 0! = 1, 1! = 1, and for n > 1, n! = n(n-1)(n-2)...1. Also n! = n·(n-1)!.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use table and recurrence to compute factorials; beware the common student error 0! = 0. Examples: 5! = 120, 7! = 5040.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complementary counting (count 'at least one' via total minus none)
rubrics_metrics.description: To count lists that must contain at least one occurrence of some symbol, compute total number of lists (with repetition allowed) and subtract the number of lists that contain none of that symbol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: number of length-4 lists from 7 letters containing at least one E is 7^4 − 6^4 = 2401 − 1296 = 1105. This often simplifies counting vs direct enumeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid double-counting; partition without overlap or use inclusion–exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: When counting by categories, ensure categories are disjoint; otherwise items may be counted multiple times (double/triple-counting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: categorizing lists by the position of a required symbol led to overcounting because lists with multiple occurrences belong to several categories. Remedy by disjoint partitioning or using inclusion–exclusion principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting subsets — combinations (n choose k)
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of k-element subsets of an n-element set, denoted (n choose k) or C(n,k), equals n!/(k!(n-k)!) when 0 ≤ k ≤ n, and equals 0 when k < 0 or k > n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive by counting k-permutations and dividing by k! (orderings of each subset). Examples: number of 5-card poker hands is 52!/(5!·47!) = 2,598,960; binomial coefficients tabulated and used throughout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pascal's identity and Pascal's triangle
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinatorial identity: C(n,k) = C(n-1,k) + C(n-1,k-1). Arranging binomial coefficients in Pascal's Triangle shows each entry (other than 1) is the sum of the two above it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combinatorial proof: classify k-subsets of an (n+1)-element set by whether they include a particular element. Use the triangle to compute coefficients recursively without factorial formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binomial theorem (coefficients equal combinations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The coefficients in the expansion of (x + y)^n are the binomial coefficients C(n,k); i.e., (x + y)^n = sum_{k=0}^n C(n,k) x^{n-k} y^k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal's Triangle rows correspond to coefficients of (x+y)^n. Use this to connect combinatorial counts with algebraic expansions and to compute coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication principle for composite independent choices (product of combination counts)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a selection consists of independent choices drawn from different pools, multiply the counts for each choice to get total possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: number of 5-card hands with two clubs and three hearts equals (13 choose 2)·(13 choose 3) = 66,924, because choose a 2-subset from 13 clubs and a 3-subset from 13 hearts then multiply.
